Nancy adds, “When we speak the blessing of God into the lives of other people, what we’re really doing is creating a setting, an opportunity in which God can actually bless those individuals.” You might think, “I’m not a priest.” She answers from the New Testament: “We have all been made priests to God… We can speak blessing into the lives of others. When we do, we actually become a channel, a conduit of God’s blessing into the lives of others.” Then she makes it personal: “One of the greatest gifts you can bestow on your husband, on your children, on your friends is the blessing of God.”

BibleProject says that in the Hebrew Bible, to “bless” is “to declare God’s life-presence over another.” John Piper tells parents that “the blessing is coming from God through Daddy,” and the same is true when a mother speaks God’s name over her children. Then comes the cloud: “Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped” (9:17). BibleProject calls the camp “an elaborate symbol of how God’s holy presence was at the center of their existence as a people.” A woman who wants God’s name on her home learns both habits: speak the Lord’s blessing out loud over her husband and children, and wait for the Lord instead of rushing ahead.

**Numbers 6:22–27 (NIV)**
22 The LORD said to Moses, 23 “Tell Aaron and his sons, ‘This is how you are to bless the Israelites. Say to them: 24 “‘“The LORD bless you and keep you; 25 the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; 26 the LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.”’ 27 “So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.”

**Numbers 9:15–23 (NIV)**
15 On the day the tabernacle, the tent of the covenant law, was set up, the cloud covered it. From evening till morning the cloud above the tabernacle looked like fire. 16 That is how it continued to be; the cloud covered it, and at night it looked like fire. 17 Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped. 18 At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at his command they encamped. As long as the cloud stayed over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. 19 When the cloud remained over the tabernacle a long time, the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order and did not set out. 20 Sometimes the cloud was over the tabernacle only a few days; at the LORD’s command they would encamp, and then at his command they would set out. 21 Sometimes the cloud stayed only from evening till morning, and when it lifted in the morning, they set out. Whether by day or by night, whenever the cloud lifted, they set out. 22 Whether the cloud stayed over the tabernacle for two days or a month or a year, the Israelites would remain in camp and not set out; but when it lifted, they would set out. 23 At the LORD’s command they encamped, and at the LORD’s command they set out. They obeyed the LORD’s order, in accordance with his command through Moses.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 6:26.** NIV: “the LORD turn his face toward you.” LSB: “Yahweh lift up His face on you.” The Hebrew is closer to the LSB. God does not merely glance your way; he lifts his face, as a father looks up with favor on his child.
- **Num 6:27.** NIV: “put my name on the Israelites.” LSB: “invoke My name on the sons of Israel.” Both are true: the priests speak God’s name over the people, and that name actually rests on them.
- **Num 9:19.** NIV: “the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order.” LSB: “the sons of Israel would keep the charge of Yahweh.” “Charge” is a duty, like a watch to be kept. Following the cloud was not a mood. It was a trust they had to keep, even when the cloud did not move for a long time.

John Piper’s interview [“How Do I Bless My Children Before Bed?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-i-bless-my-children-before-bed) at Desiring God shows how a parent’s spoken blessing becomes one of God’s means of grace. BibleProject’s [Numbers guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-numbers/) explains the blessing and the cloud of God’s presence.

**Reflection question:** God put his name on Israel, and you can speak that blessing over your home. As a woman, wife, and mother, who in your family needs to hear you speak the Lord’s blessing over them this week?

**Lesson 50: Numbers: spies, unbelief, and a forty-year delay**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God put his name on Israel and taught them to follow the cloud. Today they reach the border of the land he promised, and the test is whether they will trust him. Twelve men go in and come back with fruit and a report: the land “does flow with milk and honey” (13:27), but the people are strong and the cities are large. Caleb says, “We should go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly do it” (13:30). Ten others say they cannot, and the camp weeps and talks of going back to Egypt.

BibleProject notices that the story is told with the language of Genesis 3. The spies are sent to see whether the land is “good or bad,” and they come back holding fruit. “How the Israelites respond to the inhabitants of the garden land and whether they will trust God’s word is the test.” The podcast says, “They’ve taken the fruit and chosen not to listen to Yahweh’s words.” Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and tell the truth: “If the LORD is pleased with us, he will lead us into that land… The LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them” (14:8–9). The people talk of stoning them. God says they have refused to believe him “in spite of all the signs” (14:11). He forgives, as Moses asked, but that generation will not enter. They will wander forty years. Only Caleb, who “has a different spirit and follows me wholeheartedly” (14:24), and Joshua, will go in, along with the children the parents were so afraid of losing.

Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth puts the choice in plain words: “Everything they said was true. It was all true.” The giants were real. “Yet between the twelve spies there were two different responses to the same set of facts.” Then she says, “Where there is fear, there is not faith. Where there is faith, fear will be dissolved. You cannot walk by faith and live in fear.” A man, a husband, and a father will face some version of this report: the facts may be hard, but unbelief still treats God with contempt. The question is whether you will sound like the ten, or like Caleb.

**Numbers 13:26–14:12 (NIV)**
26 They came back to Moses and Aaron and the whole Israelite community at Kadesh in the Desert of Paran. There they reported to them and to the whole assembly and showed them the fruit of the land. 27 They gave Moses this account: “We went into the land to which you sent us, and it does flow with milk and honey! Here is its fruit. 28 But the people who live there are powerful, and the cities are fortified and very large. We even saw descendants of Anak there. 29 The Amalekites live in the Negev; the Hittites, Jebusites and Amorites live in the hill country; and the Canaanites live near the sea and along the Jordan.” 30 Then Caleb silenced the people before Moses and said, “We should go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly do it.” 31 But the men who had gone up with him said, “We can’t attack those people; they are stronger than we are.” 32 And they spread among the Israelites a bad report about the land they had explored. They said, “The land we explored devours those living in it. All the people we saw there are of great size. 33 We saw the Nephilim there (the descendants of Anak come from the Nephilim). We seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and we looked the same to them.” 1 That night all the members of the community raised their voices and wept aloud. 2 All the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron, and the whole assembly said to them, “If only we had died in Egypt! Or in this wilderness! 3 Why is the LORD bringing us to this land only to let us fall by the sword? Our wives and children will be taken as plunder. Wouldn’t it be better for us to go back to Egypt?” 4 And they said to each other, “We should choose a leader and go back to Egypt.” 5 Then Moses and Aaron fell facedown in front of the whole Israelite assembly gathered there. 6 Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had explored the land, tore their clothes 7 and said to the entire Israelite assembly, “The land we passed through and explored is exceedingly good. 8 If the LORD is pleased with us, he will lead us into that land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and will give it to us. 9 Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not be afraid of the people of the land, because we will devour them. Their protection is gone, but the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them.” 10 But the whole assembly talked about stoning them. Then the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the Israelites. 11 The LORD said to Moses, “How long will these people treat me with contempt? How long will they refuse to believe in me, in spite of all the signs I have performed among them? 12 I will strike them down with a plague and destroy them, but I will make you into a nation greater and stronger than they.”

**Numbers 14:20–25 (NIV)**
20 The LORD replied, “I have forgiven them, as you asked. 21 Nevertheless, as surely as I live and as surely as the glory of the LORD fills the whole earth, 22 not one of those who saw my glory and the signs I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness but who disobeyed me and tested me ten times— 23 not one of them will ever see the land I promised on oath to their ancestors. No one who has treated me with contempt will ever see it. 24 But because my servant Caleb has a different spirit and follows me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he went to, and his descendants will inherit it. 25 Since the Amalekites and the Canaanites are living in the valleys, turn back tomorrow and set out toward the desert along the route to the Red Sea.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 14:9.** NIV: “we will devour them.” LSB: “they are our bread.” The Hebrew is a strong picture: the enemies look huge, but to faith they are food, not a wall. Caleb is not denying the giants. He is measuring them against the Lord who is with Israel.
- **Num 14:21.** NIV: “as surely as the glory of the LORD fills the whole earth.” LSB: “all the earth will be filled with the glory of Yahweh.” The NIV reads it as an oath. The LSB (and the same words in Habakkuk 2:14) reads it as a promise: God will fill the earth with his glory, even when his people refuse to believe him.
- **Num 14:24.** NIV: “follows me wholeheartedly.” LSB: “has followed Me fully.” Both catch the point. Caleb’s “different spirit” is not a louder personality. It is a complete following.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s podcast [“Twelve Spies and the Promised Land”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/twelve-spies-and-promised-land/) shows how Numbers 13 echoes Genesis 3, and their [Numbers guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-numbers/) traces the forty-year delay. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“A Brave Look at Bad News”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/brave-look-bad-news/) at Revive Our Hearts walks through the two reports and the choice between fear and faith.

**Reflection question:** The ten spies and Caleb looked at the same land and the same giants. As a man, husband, and father, where are you tempted to take the majority’s fearful report, and what is one step of trust you will take this week because “the LORD is with us”?

**Lesson 51: Numbers: water from the rock, and the bronze serpent**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Israel refused to enter the land, and God sent that generation to wander. Today, late in those years, we come back to Kadesh and see two scenes: water from the rock, and a bronze snake on a pole. Both show how much God’s people need a better mediator than Moses, and a better cure than anything they can do for themselves.

The people quarrel again: there is no water. God tells Moses, “Speak to that rock before their eyes and it will pour out its water” (20:8). Moses gathers them, calls them rebels, and says, “Must we bring you water out of this rock?” (20:10). Then he strikes the rock twice. Water comes, but God says, “Because you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this community into the land I give them” (20:12). BibleProject is careful here: “The point of this story is not for us to walk on eggshells with Yahweh because he might punish our smallest mistake. Rather, it’s about Moses’ intentional choice to ignore God’s word.” Moses also “suggests that he and Aaron are responsible for producing the water.” The closer a leader stands to God, they say, “the higher the stakes of responsibility.” Their summary is searching: “When a human partner of God will carry out the divine will, it leads to life for others. But if we don’t have that mediator, even Moses can’t rescue us, much less ourselves.”

Soon the people grow impatient again and “detest this miserable food” (21:5). God sends venomous snakes, many die, and they confess. God does not simply take the snakes away. He tells Moses to put a bronze snake on a pole: “anyone who is bitten can look at it and live” (21:8). Jesus later says, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him” (John 3:14–15). John Piper calls the comparison shocking: “Comparing himself with a snake is shocking.” Then he explains why it fits: “The means God chooses to rescue the people from his own curse is a picture of the curse itself.” The snake on the pole “is not preventative. It is for bitten people.” “All they have to do in order to be saved from God’s wrath is look at his provision hanging on a pole.” That is the gospel you hold out to your wife and children: not that they were never bitten, but that there is life if they will look to Christ.

**Numbers 20:1–13 (NIV)**
1 In the first month the whole Israelite community arrived at the Desert of Zin, and they stayed at Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried. 2 Now there was no water for the community, and the people gathered in opposition to Moses and Aaron. 3 They quarreled with Moses and said, “If only we had died when our brothers fell dead before the LORD! 4 Why did you bring the LORD’s community into this wilderness, that we and our livestock should die here? 5 Why did you bring us up out of Egypt to this terrible place? It has no grain or figs, grapevines or pomegranates. And there is no water to drink!” 6 Moses and Aaron went from the assembly to the entrance to the tent of meeting and fell facedown, and the glory of the LORD appeared to them. 7 The LORD said to Moses, 8 “Take the staff, and you and your brother Aaron gather the assembly together. Speak to that rock before their eyes and it will pour out its water. You will bring water out of the rock for the community so they and their livestock can drink.” 9 So Moses took the staff from the LORD’s presence, just as he commanded him. 10 He and Aaron gathered the assembly together in front of the rock and Moses said to them, “Listen, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” 11 Then Moses raised his arm and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water gushed out, and the community and their livestock drank. 12 But the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this community into the land I give them.” 13 These were the waters of Meribah, where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD and where he was proved holy among them.

**Numbers 21:4–9 (NIV)**
4 They traveled from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, to go around Edom. But the people grew impatient on the way; 5 they spoke against God and against Moses, and said, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread! There is no water! And we detest this miserable food!” 6 Then the LORD sent venomous snakes among them; they bit the people and many Israelites died. 7 The people came to Moses and said, “We sinned when we spoke against the LORD and against you. Pray that the LORD will take the snakes away from us.” So Moses prayed for the people. 8 The LORD said to Moses, “Make a snake and put it up on a pole; anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.” 9 So Moses made a bronze snake and put it up on a pole. Then when anyone was bitten by a snake and looked at the bronze snake, they lived.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 20:12.** NIV: “you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy.” LSB: “you did not believe Me, to treat Me as holy.” The issue is unbelief, not a small slip in method. Moses did not treat God as holy in front of the people, and God takes that seriously in a leader.
- **Num 21:6.** NIV: “venomous snakes.” LSB: “fiery serpents.” The Hebrew can mean burning or poisonous. The older English “fiery” keeps the heat of the judgment; the NIV makes the danger plain.
- **Num 21:8.** NIV: “put it up on a pole.” LSB: “set it on a standard.” A “standard” is a banner lifted high so the whole camp can see it. That is why Jesus can say he must be “lifted up.”

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s podcast [“Why Couldn’t Moses Enter the Promised Land?”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/why-couldnt-moses-enter-promised-land/) explains why Moses struck the rock and why Israel still needed a better mediator. John Piper’s sermon [“The Son of Man Must Be Lifted Up — Like the Serpent”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-man-must-be-lifted-up-like-the-serpent) at Desiring God opens John 3:14–15 and Numbers 21 together.

**Reflection question:** Moses struck the rock and took credit; the bitten people had only to look and live. As a man, husband, and father, where do you need to honor God as holy in front of your family, and how can you help them look to Christ rather than to you?

You will bring water out of the rock for the community so they and their livestock can drink.” 9 So Moses took the staff from the LORD’s presence, just as he commanded him. 10 He and Aaron gathered the assembly together in front of the rock and Moses said to them, “Listen, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” 11 Then Moses raised his arm and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water gushed out, and the community and their livestock drank. 12 But the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this community into the land I give them.” 13 These were the waters of Meribah, where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD and where he was proved holy among them.

**Numbers 21:4–9 (NIV)**
4 They traveled from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, to go around Edom. But the people grew impatient on the way; 5 they spoke against God and against Moses, and said, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread! There is no water! And we detest this miserable food!” 6 Then the LORD sent venomous snakes among them; they bit the people and many Israelites died. 7 The people came to Moses and said, “We sinned when we spoke against the LORD and against you. Pray that the LORD will take the snakes away from us.” So Moses prayed for the people. 8 The LORD said to Moses, “Make a snake and put it up on a pole; anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.” 9 So Moses made a bronze snake and put it up on a pole. Then when anyone was bitten by a snake and looked at the bronze snake, they lived.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 20:12.** NIV: “you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy.” LSB: “you did not believe Me, to treat Me as holy.” The issue is unbelief, not a small slip in method. Moses did not treat God as holy in front of the people, and God takes that seriously in a leader.
- **Num 21:6.** NIV: “venomous snakes.” LSB: “fiery serpents.” The Hebrew can mean burning or poisonous. The older English “fiery” keeps the heat of the judgment; the NIV makes the danger plain.
- **Num 21:8.** NIV: “put it up on a pole.” LSB: “set it on a standard.” A “standard” is a banner lifted high so the whole camp can see it. That is why Jesus can say he must be “lifted up.”

BibleProject’s podcast [“Why Couldn’t Moses Enter the Promised Land?”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/why-couldnt-moses-enter-promised-land/) explains why Moses struck the rock.

**Reflection question:** The bitten people had only to look and live. As a woman, wife, and mother, where do you need to look to Christ rather than to your own efforts, and how can you help your children do the same?

**Lesson 52: Numbers: Balaam, a talking donkey, and a coming King**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we saw water from the rock and a bronze snake lifted up so the bitten could look and live. Today the story turns strange and wonderful. Balak, king of Moab, hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam goes, and “the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him” (22:22). The donkey sees the angel three times. Balaam does not. He beats the animal until the Lord opens the donkey’s mouth, then opens Balaam’s eyes. The angel says, “your path is a reckless one before me” (22:32), and then, “Go with the men, but speak only what I tell you” (22:35).

BibleProject says this odd scene “fits a larger pattern. Sometimes God uses unusual means to capture the attention of a prophet—a burning bush… or even a talking donkey!” Balaam’s “lack of spiritual awareness is not overcome until God opens his eyes.” Balak wants a curse, but “since Balaam is permitted to speak only as God instructs him, he can only declare blessings over Israel.” In the last oracle we hear this morning, Balaam’s eyes are opened again, and he sees a King: “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob; a scepter will rise out of Israel” (24:17). “A ruler will come out of Jacob” (24:19). BibleProject says Balaam’s poems “predict a messiah-king who will come from Israel to reign over all nations,” and that even while Israel grumbles, “Yahweh blesses them and promises future deliverance and blessing in the form of the coming messiah.”

That promise lands close to Christmas. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, teaching on the star of Bethlehem, takes us back to this very text. “Balaam was a pagan prophet who, in an unusual way, was used by God.” She says “there was a prophecy of a star coming that would be a signal that a King was rising out of Israel, and this King would have authority, not just over Israel, but over all the nations of the earth.” The wise men “may well have known this prophecy.” God would not let a hired curse stand, and he would not let his people miss the King. A father can tell his children: the star over Bethlehem was not a surprise to Scripture. Numbers already said he was coming.

**Numbers 22:21–35 (NIV)**
21 Balaam got up in the morning, saddled his donkey and went with the Moabite officials. 22 But God was very angry when he went, and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him. Balaam was riding on his donkey, and his two servants were with him. 23 When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, it turned off the road into a field. Balaam beat it to get it back on the road. 24 Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path through the vineyards, with walls on both sides. 25 When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, it pressed close to the wall, crushing Balaam’s foot against it. So he beat the donkey again. 26 Then the angel of the LORD moved on ahead and stood in a narrow place where there was no room to turn, either to the right or to the left. 27 When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, it lay down under Balaam, and he was angry and beat it with his staff. 28 Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth, and it said to Balaam, “What have I done to you to make you beat me these three times?” 29 Balaam answered the donkey, “You have made a fool of me! If only I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now.” 30 The donkey said to Balaam, “Am I not your own donkey, which you have always ridden, to this day? Have I been in the habit of doing this to you?” “No,” he said. 31 Then the LORD opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with his sword drawn. So he bowed low and fell facedown. 32 The angel of the LORD asked him, “Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I have come here to oppose you because your path is a reckless one before me. 33 The donkey saw me and turned away from me these three times. If it had not turned away, I would certainly have killed you by now, but I would have spared it.” 34 Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, “I have sinned. I did not realize you were standing in the road to oppose me. Now if you are displeased, I will go back.” 35 The angel of the LORD said to Balaam, “Go with the men, but speak only what I tell you.” So Balaam went with Balak’s officials.

**Numbers 24:15–19 (NIV)**
15 Then he spoke his message: “The prophecy of Balaam son of Beor, the prophecy of one whose eye sees clearly, 16 the prophecy of one who hears the words of God, who has knowledge from the Most High, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who falls prostrate, and whose eyes are opened: 17 “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come out of Jacob; a scepter will rise out of Israel. He will crush the foreheads of Moab, the skulls of all the people of Sheth. 18 Edom will be conquered; Seir, his enemy, will be conquered, but Israel will grow strong. 19 A ruler will come out of Jacob and destroy the survivors of the city.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 22:32.** NIV: “your path is a reckless one before me.” LSB: “your way was contrary to me.” Both are true. Balaam’s road was not only careless. It was against the Lord, and the angel stood in it as an adversary until Balaam’s eyes were opened.
- **Num 24:15.** NIV: “the prophecy of one whose eye sees clearly.” LSB: “the oracle of the man whose eye is uncovered.” The gift is not that Balaam is naturally sharp. God uncovers his eye, just as he opened his eyes on the road.
- **Num 24:19.** NIV: “A ruler will come out of Jacob.” LSB: “one from Jacob shall have dominion.” The LSB keeps the note of reign. This is not only a leader for Israel. He will have dominion.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Numbers guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-numbers/) and the podcast [“Why Couldn’t Moses Enter the Promised Land?”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/why-couldnt-moses-enter-promised-land/) tell the Balaam story and the promise of a coming messiah-king. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“The Star”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/star/) at Revive Our Hearts connects Numbers 24:17 to the star that led the wise men to Jesus.

**Reflection question:** God stood in Balaam’s reckless path and still brought a blessing and a promise of the King. As a man, husband, and father, where might the Lord be blocking a path of yours for your good, and how will you help your children see that the Christmas star was already promised in Numbers?

**Lesson 53: Deuteronomy: hear, O Israel — remember and obey**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday a hired curse became a blessing, and Balaam saw a King: “A star will come out of Jacob.” Today we open Deuteronomy. Moses stands before the children of the wilderness generation, on the edge of the land, and begins, “Now, Israel, hear the decrees and laws I am about to teach you. Follow them so that you may live” (4:1). This lesson falls on Christmas Eve, a good night to do what Moses says next: remember what God has done, and teach it to your children.

BibleProject says Deuteronomy is “Moses’ final word to Israel, encouraging the people to listen to God and love him.” The book’s first charge is “hear,” and they explain that the Hebrew word *shema* “means more than simply ‘hear.’ Its meaning includes responding to what you hear. In English we would say ‘obey.’” Moses tells them that careful obedience will show the nations “wisdom and understanding” (4:6). BibleProject puts the point this way: “Israel has the chance to show the world the ‘wisdom and justice of God.’” And the reason is close and personal: “What other nation is so great as to have their gods near them the way the LORD our God is near us whenever we pray to him?” (4:7). Then the heart of the lesson: “Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen or let them fade from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and to their children after them” (4:9).

John Piper calls this “the solemn duty of all parents.” “The most important school a child should ever attend is the home. And the most influential theological teachers he should ever have are Mom and Dad.” He notes that Deuteronomy 4:9 is “a word to grandparents too.” Then he says, “God’s design for the preservation of historical revelation is the family. Within the Christian community the main link between what this generation knows and what the next generation will know is the link between parent and child.” If parents let that fade, “we serve not only their ignorance and unbelief, but also their destruction.” Moses ends the reading with the same truth: you were shown these things “so that you might know that the LORD is God; besides him there is no other” (4:35). “Acknowledge and take to heart this day” (4:39), and keep his commands “so that it may go well with you and your children after you” (4:40). On Christmas Eve, a father can look his children in the eye and tell them what God has done—from Egypt to the manger—and why there is no other.

**Deuteronomy 4:1–14 (NIV)**
1 Now, Israel, hear the decrees and laws I am about to teach you. Follow them so that you may live and may go in and take possession of the land the LORD, the God of your ancestors, is giving you. 2 Do not add to what I command you and do not subtract from it, but keep the commands of the LORD your God that I give you. 3 You saw with your own eyes what the LORD did at Baal Peor. The LORD your God destroyed from among you everyone who followed the Baal of Peor, 4 but all of you who held fast to the LORD your God are still alive today. 5 See, I have taught you decrees and laws as the LORD my God commanded me, so that you may follow them in the land you are entering to take possession of it. 6 Observe them carefully, for this will show your wisdom and understanding to the nations, who will hear about all these decrees and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” 7 What other nation is so great as to have their gods near them the way the LORD our God is near us whenever we pray to him? 8 And what other nation is so great as to have such righteous decrees and laws as this body of laws I am setting before you today? 9 Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen or let them fade from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and to their children after them. 10 Remember the day you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, when he said to me, “Assemble the people before me to hear my words so that they may learn to revere me as long as they live in the land and may teach them to their children.” 11 You came near and stood at the foot of the mountain while it blazed with fire to the very heavens, with black clouds and deep darkness. 12 Then the LORD spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of words but saw no form; there was only a voice. 13 He declared to you his covenant, the Ten Commandments, which he commanded you to follow and then wrote them on two stone tablets. 14 And the LORD directed me at that time to teach you the decrees and laws you are to follow in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.

**Deuteronomy 4:32–40 (NIV)**
32 Ask now about the former days, long before your time, from the day God created human beings on the earth; ask from one end of the heavens to the other. Has anything so great as this ever happened, or has anything like it ever been heard of? 33 Has any other people heard the voice of God speaking out of fire, as you have, and lived? 34 Has any god ever tried to take for himself one nation out of another nation, by testings, by signs and wonders, by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, or by great and awesome deeds, like all the things the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your very eyes? 35 You were shown these things so that you might know that the LORD is God; besides him there is no other. 36 From heaven he made you hear his voice to discipline you. On earth he showed you his great fire, and you heard his words from out of the fire. 37 Because he loved your ancestors and chose their descendants after them, he brought you out of Egypt by his Presence and his great strength, 38 to drive out before you nations greater and stronger than you and to bring you into their land to give it to you for your inheritance, as it is today. 39 Acknowledge and take to heart this day that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below. There is no other. 40 Keep his decrees and commands, which I am giving you today, so that it may go well with you and your children after you and that you may live long in the land the LORD your God gives you for all time.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 4:1.** NIV: “hear the decrees and laws.” LSB: “listen to the statutes and the judgments.” The Hebrew word is *shema*. BibleProject notes that it means more than sound in the ear; it means to hear and respond. The LSB’s “listen” helps make that clear.
- **Deut 4:9.** NIV: “watch yourselves closely” and “let them fade from your heart.” LSB: “keep your soul very carefully” and “lest they depart from your heart.” The danger is not only a weak memory. It is a soul that stops guarding what God has done.
- **Deut 4:37.** NIV: “he brought you out of Egypt by his Presence.” LSB: “He personally brought you from Egypt.” The Hebrew points to God himself going with them. Rescue is not a distant idea. God came near.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s sermon [“Will the Next Generation Know?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/will-the-next-generation-know) at Desiring God opens Deuteronomy 4:9 and the duty of parents and grandparents. BibleProject’s [Deuteronomy guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-deuteronomy/) explains *shema* and how Israel’s obedience was meant to show the nations who God is.

**Reflection question:** Moses said, “Teach them to your children and to their children after them.” As a man, husband, and father, what is one thing God has done that you will tell your children this Christmas Eve, so it does not fade from their hearts?

32 Ask now about the former days, long before your time, from the day God created human beings on the earth; ask from one end of the heavens to the other. Has anything so great as this ever happened, or has anything like it ever been heard of? 33 Has any other people heard the voice of God speaking out of fire, as you have, and lived? 34 Has any god ever tried to take for himself one nation out of another nation, by testings, by signs and wonders, by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, or by great and awesome deeds, like all the things the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your very eyes? 35 You were shown these things so that you might know that the LORD is God; besides him there is no other. 36 From heaven he made you hear his voice to discipline you. On earth he showed you his great fire, and you heard his words from out of the fire. 37 Because he loved your ancestors and chose their descendants after them, he brought you out of Egypt by his Presence and his great strength, 38 to drive out before you nations greater and stronger than you and to bring you into their land to give it to you for your inheritance, as it is today. 39 Acknowledge and take to heart this day that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below. There is no other. 40 Keep his decrees and commands, which I am giving you today, so that it may go well with you and your children after you and that you may live long in the land the LORD your God gives you for all time.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 4:1.** NIV: “hear the decrees and laws.” LSB: “listen to the statutes and the judgments.” The Hebrew word is *shema*. BibleProject notes that it means more than sound in the ear; it means to hear and respond. The LSB’s “listen” helps make that clear.
- **Deut 4:9.** NIV: “watch yourselves closely” and “let them fade from your heart.” LSB: “keep your soul very carefully” and “lest they depart from your heart.” The danger is not only a weak memory. It is a soul that stops guarding what God has done.
- **Deut 4:37.** NIV: “he brought you out of Egypt by his Presence.” LSB: “He personally brought you from Egypt.” The Hebrew points to God himself going with them. Rescue is not a distant idea. God came near.

**Go deeper:** Barbara Reaoch’s [“Ask an Older Woman: How to Disciple Long-Distance Grandchildren”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/blog/ask-older-woman-1-how-disciple-long-distance-grand/) at Revive Our Hearts opens Deuteronomy 4:9 for women who want to pass a living faith to the next generation. John Piper’s sermon [“Will the Next Generation Know?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/will-the-next-generation-know) at Desiring God shows why the home is the first school. BibleProject’s [Deuteronomy guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-deuteronomy/) explains *shema* and Moses’ call to listen and love.

**Reflection question:** Moses said, “Teach them to your children and to their children after them.” As a woman, wife, and mother, what is one thing God has done that you will tell your children this Christmas Eve, so it does not fade from their hearts?

**Lesson 54: Deuteronomy: love the Lord with all your heart**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses told Israel to hear, remember, and teach their children. Today he comes to the center of the book, and of the faith: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (6:4–5). This lesson falls on Christmas Day. The greatest commandment is not a cold rule. It is a call to love the God who first loved us and came near.

BibleProject notes that this line, the Shema, “became an important daily prayer in Judaism, and it brings all the themes of the book together.” The word *shema*, they say, “means to allow the words to sink in, provide understanding, and generate a response—it’s about action. In Hebrew, hearing and doing are the same thing.” And love, the Hebrew word *ahavah*, “is not about the warm, fuzzy, emotional energy we feel when we like someone. Much like listening, biblical love is about action.” Israel is to love God “with all of their beings.” Jesus later called this “the first and greatest commandment” (Matt 22:37–38).

John Piper says, “The first assignment a parent has after loving God is to store God’s Word in his heart and teach it to his children.” That is exactly the order of verses 5–7. The words are to be “on your hearts” (6:6), then: “Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (6:7). Moses also warns the other side of a full table: when you eat and are satisfied in a land you did not build, “be careful that you do not forget the LORD, who brought you out of Egypt” (6:12). Christmas morning, with gifts and a full house, is a good time for a father to love God out loud, and to talk of him with his children in the ordinary places of the day, so that satisfaction does not become forgetfulness.

**Deuteronomy 6:1–15 (NIV)**
1 These are the commands, decrees and laws the LORD your God directed me to teach you to observe in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess, 2 so that you, your children and their children after them may fear the LORD your God as long as you live by keeping all his decrees and commands that I give you, and so that you may enjoy long life. 3 Hear, Israel, and be careful to obey so that it may go well with you and that you may increase greatly in a land flowing with milk and honey, just as the LORD, the God of your ancestors, promised you. 4 Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. 5 Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates. 10 When the LORD your God brings you into the land he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give you—a land with large, flourishing cities you did not build, 11 houses filled with all kinds of good things you did not provide, wells you did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves you did not plant—then when you eat and are satisfied, 12 be careful that you do not forget the LORD, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. 13 Fear the LORD your God, serve him only and take your oaths in his name. 14 Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you; 15 for the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God and his anger will burn against you, and he will destroy you from the face of the land.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 6:5.** NIV: “with all your strength.” LSB: “with all your might.” Both try to catch a Hebrew word for muchness, the whole of your capacity. Love for God is not a corner of life. It takes all of you.
- **Deut 6:7.** NIV: “Impress them on your children.” LSB: “You shall teach them diligently to your sons.” The Hebrew verb has the sense of sharpening, repeating, pressing the words in. This is not a one-time talk. It is careful, regular teaching.
- **Deut 6:12.** NIV: “out of the land of slavery.” LSB: “out of the house of slavery.” The LSB is more literal. Egypt was not only a country. It was a house that held them. Remembering the Lord means remembering who broke them out.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s article [“What’s the Meaning of the Jewish Shema Prayer in the Bible?”](https://bibleproject.com/articles/what-is-the-shema/) by Tim Mackie explains *shema* and *ahavah*. John Piper’s sermon [“Will the Next Generation Know?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/will-the-next-generation-know) at Desiring God shows how Deuteronomy 6 makes the home the first place the next generation learns to love God.

**Reflection question:** The first assignment after loving God is to store his Word in your heart and teach it to your children. As a man, husband, and father, where in the ordinary rhythm of this Christmas Day will you talk of the Lord with your family, so that a full table does not become a forgetful heart?

**Lesson 55: Deuteronomy: do not forget the Lord in the land**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses called Israel to love the Lord with all their heart, and warned them not to forget him when they were full. Today he presses that warning deeper. God led them forty years in the wilderness “to humble and test you in order to know what was in your heart” (8:2). He let them hunger, then fed them with manna, “to teach you that man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (8:3). Then comes the good land, and the danger: “When you have eaten and are satisfied, praise the LORD your God” (8:10). “Be careful that you do not forget the LORD your God” (8:11). This lesson falls on the day after Christmas, when the table has been full. It is a good day to hear this.

John Piper takes us from Deuteronomy 8 to Jesus in the wilderness. Jesus was hungry, and Satan told him to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered with this very verse. Piper says God gave Israel manna, “an utterly un-heard-of food falling from heaven,” so that “they would learn to live on everything that comes from the mouth of God.” Manna, he says, is “one of the incredible ways God can, with a mere word, reveal himself and meet your needs when all else looks hopeless.” But the lesson is not “expect a miracle snack whenever you want one.” Piper hears Jesus say to the devil, “Don’t trust in bread—not even miracle bread—trust in God. Don’t get your deepest satisfactions in life from food—not even God-wrought miracle food—but from God.” “Every word that comes out of the mouth of God reveals God. And it is this self-revelation that we feed on.”

That is why forgetting is so serious once the land is rich. Moses says you may build fine houses, see your silver and gold increase, and then say, “My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me” (8:17). The answer is verse 18: “But remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you the ability to produce wealth.” A man, a husband, and a father can feed his family well and still starve their souls if bread becomes the point. Remember who carried you through the hard stretch, and who filled the table yesterday. Then praise him, and live on his word.

**Deuteronomy 8:1–18 (NIV)**
1 Be careful to follow every command I am giving you today, so that you may live and increase and may enter and possess the land the LORD promised on oath to your ancestors. 2 Remember how the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness these forty years, to humble and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep his commands. 3 He humbled you, causing you to hunger and then feeding you with manna, which neither you nor your ancestors had known, to teach you that man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. 4 Your clothes did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years. 5 Know then in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you. 6 Observe the commands of the LORD your God, walking in obedience to him and revering him. 7 For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land—a land with brooks, streams, and deep springs gushing out into the valleys and hills; 8 a land with wheat and barley, vines and fig trees, pomegranates, olive oil and honey; 9 a land where bread will not be scarce and you will lack nothing; a land where the rocks are iron and you can dig copper out of the hills. 10 When you have eaten and are satisfied, praise the LORD your God for the good land he has given you. 11 Be careful that you do not forget the LORD your God, failing to observe his commands, his laws and his decrees that I am giving you this day. 12 Otherwise, when you eat and are satisfied, when you build fine houses and settle down, 13 and when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all you have is multiplied, 14 then your heart will become proud and you will forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. 15 He led you through the vast and dreadful wilderness, that thirsty and waterless land, with its venomous snakes and scorpions. He brought you water out of hard rock. 16 He gave you manna to eat in the wilderness, something your ancestors had never known, to humble and test you so that in the end it might go well with you. 17 You may say to yourself, “My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me.” 18 But remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you the ability to produce wealth, and so confirms his covenant, which he swore to your ancestors, as it is today.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 8:10.** NIV: “praise the LORD your God.” LSB: “you shall bless Yahweh your God.” The Hebrew is “bless.” Praise thanks God. Blessing God is a spoken return of honor to the one who filled you.
- **Deut 8:14.** NIV: “your heart will become proud.” LSB: “your heart becomes lifted up.” The picture is a heart that rises, as if it no longer needs the God who carried it through the wilderness.
- **Deut 8:17–18.** NIV: “the strength of my hands have produced this wealth” / “the ability to produce wealth.” LSB: “the might of my hand made me this wealth” / “power to make wealth.” Both make the same sharp contrast: you did not make this. God gave the power.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s sermon [“Man Shall Not Live on Bread Alone”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/man-shall-not-live-on-bread-alone) at Desiring God reads Deuteronomy 8:2–3 with Jesus in the wilderness, and shows why we are to trust God, not bread.

**Reflection question:** Moses warned that a full table can make a man say, “My power produced this.” As a man, husband, and father, where are you tempted to take credit for what God has given your family, and how will you remember him and live on his word this week?

**Lesson 56: Deuteronomy: a prophet like Moses, and choose life**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses warned Israel not to forget the Lord when the table was full. Today he points them to a Prophet they must hear, and to a choice they must make. “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your fellow Israelites. You must listen to him” (18:15). God says, “I will put my words in his mouth” (18:18), and “I myself will call to account anyone who does not listen” (18:19). Then, at the end of the book, Moses sets the choice in the open: “I have set before you life and death, blessings and curses. Now choose life, so that you and your children may live” (30:19). “For the LORD is your life” (30:20).

John Piper follows the apostle Peter to this promise. In Acts 3, Peter tells the crowd that Moses said God would raise up a prophet like himself, and “You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.” Piper says, “With the coming of Jesus Christ into the world the days of fulfillment, proclaimed by all the prophets, began. And ever since the first Christmas we have been living in those days.” “The first Christmas is history. The Messiah has come.” So the word is not far off. “No, the word is very near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart so you may obey it” (30:14). BibleProject hears Moses force the decision: “So choose life, by loving the Lord your God and listening to him.” They also note Moses’ hope that God would one day “transform the hearts of his people, so that they can actually listen to and love God from the heart and discover true life.”

That Prophet has come, and the choice is still the same. Listen to Jesus, hold fast to him, and choose life for yourself and for your children. A man, a husband, and a father cannot make that choice for his household in their place. But he can listen first, and then lead them to the Prophet whose words are life.

**Deuteronomy 18:15–22 (NIV)**
15 The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your fellow Israelites. **Lesson 57: Deuteronomy: be strong and courageous — Moses dies, Joshua rises**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses promised a prophet like himself, and called Israel to choose life. Today the baton is passed. Moses is 120 years old, and the Lord has said he will not cross the Jordan. But the people are not left alone. “The LORD your God himself will cross over ahead of you” (31:3), and “Joshua also will cross over ahead of you” (31:3). Moses tells all Israel, and then Joshua in their sight, “Be strong and courageous… for the LORD your God goes with you; he will never leave you nor forsake you” (31:6). Then Moses climbs Mount Nebo, sees the land, and dies there as the servant of the Lord. God buries him. Joshua is filled with the spirit of wisdom, and the book closes with this: “no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (34:10).

BibleProject says the narrators want us to know “there was no other leader like Moses (despite Joshua’s great leadership).” That line looks back, and it also looks ahead. “With this knowledge, we can look forward with hope to a coming prophet and leader who will be even greater than Moses, the suffering servant who will die on behalf of God’s people.” Yesterday we heard that promise. Today we see why it matters: even the greatest servant dies, and the people still need a better leader. John Piper takes the repeated command, “Be strong and courageous,” and asks whether a Christian can hold that promise. His answer is yes, in Christ. The ground of it, he says, is the last clause: “The reason that you can be strong and be courageous and not fear and not be dismayed is that the Lord is going to be with you wherever you go.” So “be strong means be strong in the strength of the Lord.” “The bottom line is that this is a call to faith — faith in the promised strength of God.”

A man, a husband, and a father will also face work that is bigger than he is. Moses could not cross, and Joshua could not go in his own strength. The courage God commands is not swagger. It is trusting that the Lord himself goes before you, and then taking the next step with your family.

**Deuteronomy 31:1–8 (NIV)**
1 Then Moses went out and spoke these words to all Israel: 2 “I am now a hundred and twenty years old and I am no longer able to lead you. The LORD has said to me, ‘You shall not cross the Jordan.’ 3 The LORD your God himself will cross over ahead of you. He will destroy these nations before you, and you will take possession of their land. Joshua also will cross over ahead of you, as the LORD said. 4 And the LORD will do to them what he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, whom he destroyed along with their land. 5 The LORD will deliver them to you, and you must do to them all that I have commanded you. 6 Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or terrified because of them, for the LORD your God goes with you; he will never leave you nor forsake you.” 7 Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the presence of all Israel, “Be strong and courageous, for you must go with this people into the land that the LORD swore to their ancestors to give them, and you must divide it among them as their inheritance. 8 The LORD himself goes before you and will be with you; he will never leave you nor forsake you. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged.”

**Deuteronomy 34:1–12 (NIV)**
1 Then Moses climbed Mount Nebo from the plains of Moab to the top of Pisgah, across from Jericho. There the LORD showed him the whole land—from Gilead to Dan, 2 all of Naphtali, the territory of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the Mediterranean Sea, 3 the Negev and the whole region from the Valley of Jericho, the City of Palms, as far as Zoar. 4 Then the LORD said to him, “This is the land I promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when I said, ‘I will give it to your descendants.’ I have let you see it with your eyes, but you will not cross over into it.” 5 And Moses the servant of the LORD died there in Moab, as the LORD had said. 6 He buried him in Moab, in the valley opposite Beth Peor, but to this day no one knows where his grave is. 7 Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak nor his strength gone. 8 The Israelites grieved for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the time of weeping and mourning was over. 9 Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites listened to him and did what the LORD had commanded Moses. 10 Since then, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, 11 who did all those signs and wonders the LORD sent him to do in Egypt—to Pharaoh and to all his officials and to his whole land. 12 For no one has ever shown the mighty power or performed the awesome deeds that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 31:6, 8.** NIV: “he will never leave you nor forsake you.” LSB: “He will not fail you or forsake you.” “Fail” is a strong word. God will not drop Joshua, and he will not walk away.
- **Deut 34:5.** NIV: “as the LORD had said.” LSB: “according to the command of Yahweh.” Moses’ death is not an accident at the border. It is under God’s word, as we saw when Moses struck the rock at Meribah.
- **Deut 34:10.** NIV: “no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses.” LSB: “there has not yet arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses.” The little word “yet” keeps the door open. The book ends by making us wait for the prophet like Moses.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s [“Be Strong and Courageous in Jesus”](https://www.desiringgod.org/be-strong-and-courageous-in-jesus) at Desiring God shows why a Christian can hold this promise in Christ, and why “be strong” means strength the Lord supplies. BibleProject’s [Deuteronomy guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-deuteronomy/) and the podcast [“Deuteronomy: Moses’ Final Words”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/moses-final-words/) reflect on Moses’ death and the hope of a greater prophet.

**Reflection question:** Moses died, and Joshua still had to be strong and courageous because the Lord went with him. As a man, husband, and father, where is God asking you to take a step that is bigger than you, and how will you trust his presence instead of your own strength?

**Lesson 58: Joshua: be strong — Rahab hides the spies**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses died on Mount Nebo, and Joshua rose to lead. Today the Lord speaks to Joshua himself: “Moses my servant is dead. Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan” (1:2). The charge we heard yesterday is given again, three times in nine verses: “Be strong and courageous.” But a new line is added. Courage is not a feeling Joshua must invent. It is tied to the Book of the Law: “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night… Then you will be prosperous and successful” (1:8). “Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go” (1:9).

BibleProject notes that “the author intentionally presents Joshua as a new Moses,” and that “God calls him to courageously follow his instructions.” Then Joshua does what Moses once did: he sends spies. “Things go much better this time, and even some Canaanites, such as Rahab the prostitute, turn to follow the God of Israel.” Rahab hides the men, and she tells them why: “I know that the LORD has given you this land… for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below” (2:9, 11). John Piper asks why she did this. She had heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea. “God had Rahab’s salvation in mind when he split the Red Sea.” His mighty acts were meant to lead people like her “to humble themselves before Yahweh, stop putting up their rebellion against the true God, and embrace him and be saved.” Hebrews 11:31 says, “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed with those who were disobedient.”

A man, a husband, and a father is called to the same two movements we see today. Take God at his word, and keep it on your lips at home. And notice that the first “victory” in Joshua is not a wall falling, but a household being shown kindness because one woman believed.

**Joshua 1:1–9 (NIV)**
1 After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ aide: 2 “Moses my servant is dead. Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan River into the land I am about to give to them—to the Israelites. 3 I will give you every place where you set your foot, as I promised Moses. 4 Your territory will extend from the desert to Lebanon, and from the great river, the Euphrates—all the Hittite country—to the Mediterranean Sea in the west. 5 No one will be able to stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you. 6 Be strong and courageous, because you will lead these people to inherit the land I swore to their ancestors to give them. 7 “Be strong and very courageous. Be careful to obey all the law my servant Moses gave you; do not turn from it to the right or to the left, that you may be successful wherever you go. 8 Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful. 9 Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”

**Joshua 2:1–14 (NIV)**
1 Then Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two spies from Shittim. “Go, look over the land,” he said, “especially Jericho.” So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there. 2 The king of Jericho was told, “Look, some of the Israelites have come here tonight to spy out the land.” 3 So the king of Jericho sent this message to Rahab: “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, because they have come to spy out the whole land.” 4 But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. She said, “Yes, the men came to me, but I did not know where they had come from. 5 At dusk, when it was time to close the city gate, they left. I don’t know which way they went. Go after them quickly. You may catch up with them.” 6 (But she had taken them up to the roof and hidden them under the stalks of flax she had laid out on the roof.) 7 So the men set out in pursuit of the spies on the road that leads to the fords of the Jordan, and as soon as the pursuers had gone out, the gate was shut. 8 Before the spies lay down for the night, she went up on the roof 9 and said to them, “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that a great fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who live in this country are melting in fear because of you. 10 We have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea for you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites east of the Jordan, whom you completely destroyed. 11 When we heard of it, our hearts melted in fear and everyone’s courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below. 12 “Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that you will show kindness to my family, because I have shown kindness to you. Give me a sure sign 13 that you will spare the lives of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them—and that you will save us from death.” 14 “Our lives for your lives!” the men assured her. “If you don’t tell what we are doing, we will treat you kindly and faithfully when the LORD gives us the land.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**

**Lesson 58: Joshua: be strong — Rahab hides the spies**

Good morning. Yesterday Moses died on Mount Nebo, and Joshua rose to lead. Today the Lord speaks to Joshua himself: “Moses my servant is dead. Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan” (1:2). The charge we heard yesterday is given again, three times in nine verses: “Be strong and courageous.” But a new line is added. Courage is not a feeling Joshua must invent. It is tied to the Book of the Law: “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night… Then you will be prosperous and successful” (1:8). “Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go” (1:9).

Then Joshua does what Moses once did: he sends spies. This time a woman in Jericho hides them, and she tells them why: “I know that the LORD has given you this land… for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below” (2:9, 11). Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth hears Hebrews 11 name her in the “Hall of Faith,” alongside Sarah. “I love that phrase. Rahab the prostitute—parenthesis implied, who deserved to perish—did not perish!” How was she saved? “She was saved by faith. The grace of God came to her, and she received it by faith. Her willingness to express hospitality to the spies was an evidence of her faith.” Nancy is careful: “She was not saved because she harbored the spies. She was saved because she believed in God. And the evidence that she believed God was that she harbored the spies.”

John Piper asks why she did this. She had heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea. “God had Rahab’s salvation in mind when he split the Red Sea.” His mighty acts were meant to lead people like her “to humble themselves before Yahweh… and embrace him and be saved.” Hebrews 11:31 says, “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed with those who were disobedient.” A wife and mother can hear, in Rahab’s plea for her father’s house, a faith that does not stop with herself. She asks the Lord for kindness that would cover her family, and she risks her life to act on what she believes.

**Joshua 1:1–9 (NIV)**
1 After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ aide: 2 “Moses my servant is dead. Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan River into the land I am about to give to them—to the Israelites. 3 I will give you every place where you set your foot, as I promised Moses. 4 Your territory will extend from the desert to Lebanon, and from the great river, the Euphrates—all the Hittite country—to the Mediterranean Sea in the west. 5 No one will be able to stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you. 6 Be strong and courageous, because you will lead these people to inherit the land I swore to their ancestors to give them. 7 “Be strong and very courageous. Be careful to obey all the law my servant Moses gave you; do not turn from it to the right or to the left, that you may be successful wherever you go. 8 Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful. 9 Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”

**Joshua 2:1–14 (NIV)**
1 Then Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two spies from Shittim. “Go, look over the land,” he said, “especially Jericho.” So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there. 2 The king of Jericho was told, “Look, some of the Israelites have come here tonight to spy out the land.” 3 So the king of Jericho sent this message to Rahab: “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, because they have come to spy out the whole land.” 4 But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. She said, “Yes, the men came to me, but I did not know where they had come from. 5 At dusk, when it was time to close the city gate, they left. I don’t know which way they went. Go after them quickly. You may catch up with them.” 6 (But she had taken them up to the roof and hidden them under the stalks of flax she had laid out on the roof.) 7 So the men set out in pursuit of the spies on the road that leads to the fords of the Jordan, and as soon as the pursuers had gone out, the gate was shut. 8 Before the spies lay down for the night, she went up on the roof 9 and said to them, “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that a great fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who live in this country are melting in fear because of you. 10 We have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea for you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites east of the Jordan, whom you completely destroyed. 11 When we heard of it, our hearts melted in fear and everyone’s courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below. 12 “Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that you will show kindness to my family, because I have shown kindness to you. Give me a sure sign 13 that you will spare the lives of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them—and that you will save us from death.” 14 “Our lives for your lives!” the men assured her. “If you don’t tell what we are doing, we will treat you kindly and faithfully when the LORD gives us the land.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Josh 1:8.** NIV: “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips.” LSB: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth.” The law is not only for private reading. It is to stay in Joshua’s speech as he leads.
- **Josh 2:12, 14.** NIV: “kindness” and “kindly and faithfully.” LSB: “lovingkindness” and “lovingkindness and truth.” Rahab is asking for covenant loyalty, the faithful love of the Lord, not a small favor. She wants her father’s house brought under that same kindness.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“The Legacy of Rahab”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/legacy-rahab/) at Revive Our Hearts shows that Rahab was saved by faith, and that hiding the spies was the evidence of that faith. John Piper’s interview [“God’s Fame and Global Missions”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/gods-fame-and-global-missions) at Desiring God traces her faith back to what she heard about the Red Sea. BibleProject’s [Joshua guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-joshua/) presents Joshua as a new Moses, and Rahab as one who turns to follow Israel’s God.

**Reflection question:** God told Joshua to be strong by keeping the Book of the Law on his lips, and Rahab hid the spies because she believed the Lord is God in heaven and on earth. As a woman, wife, and mother, where is God asking you to take him at his word and take a costly stand of faith for your household?

lessons.title: Joshua: through the Jordan, and the walls of Jericho

sources.label: John Piper, Faith to Be Strong and Faith to Be Weak (Desiring God, Aug 10, 1997)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 59: Joshua: through the Jordan, and the walls of Jericho**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Rahab hid the spies and confessed that the Lord is God in heaven and on earth. Today that confession is put to the test in the river and at the wall. The Jordan is at flood stage, but the priests carrying the ark step in first. “As soon as the priests who carried the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water’s edge, the water from upstream stopped flowing” (3:15–16). The people cross on dry ground, with the ark standing in the middle until the whole nation is over. Then Jericho is shut tight. The Lord says to Joshua, “See, I have delivered Jericho into your hands” (6:2)—before a wall has moved. The battle plan is a march, trumpets, six days of silence, and a shout on the seventh. “When the trumpets sounded, the army shouted… the wall collapsed” (6:20). And in the middle of the command, yesterday’s promise is kept: “Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall be spared, because she hid the spies we sent” (6:17).

BibleProject says the river parts “just as the sea parted for Moses in Exodus,” and that Joshua “does so, even when God’s instructions don’t make sense from a human perspective.” The city falls because he obeys. This is not Israel’s cleverness. “This story will not be about the Israelites versus the Canaanites. Rather, it is God’s battle.” John Piper reads Hebrews 11:30 beside the Red Sea and says, “Through our faith God can and does work miracles and acts of providence to bring practical earthly help and deliverance to his people.” The walls of Jericho are one of those miracles: “God breaks into the normal way things work and in an extraordinary way makes them work differently.” Hebrews 11:30 says, “By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the army had marched around them for seven days.” Piper is careful, later in the same sermon, to add that God does not always work that way to spare his people from suffering. Faith is not a lever. It is trust in the God who goes first.

A man, a husband, and a father will also face rivers that look too high and walls that will not open. The call is the same: step where the Lord has already gone ahead, keep his word even when the plan looks foolish, and wait for him to do what only he can do.

**Joshua 3:14–17 (NIV)**
14 So when the people broke camp to cross the Jordan, the priests carrying the ark of the covenant went ahead of them. 15 Now the Jordan is at flood stage all during harvest. Yet as soon as the priests who carried the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water’s edge, 16 the water from upstream stopped flowing. It piled up in a heap a great distance away, at a town called Adam in the vicinity of Zarethan, while the water flowing down to the Sea of the Arabah (that is, the Dead Sea) was completely cut off. So the people crossed over opposite Jericho. 17 The priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD stopped in the middle of the Jordan and stood on dry ground, while all Israel passed by until the whole nation had completed the crossing on dry ground.

**Joshua 6:1–20 (NIV)**
1 Now the gates of Jericho were securely barred because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in. 2 Then the LORD said to Joshua, “See, I have delivered Jericho into your hands, along with its king and its fighting men. 3 March around the city once with all the armed men. Do this for six days. 4 Have seven priests carry trumpets of rams’ horns in front of the ark. On the seventh day, march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the trumpets. 5 When you hear them sound a long blast on the trumpets, have the whole army give a loud shout; then the wall of the city will collapse and the army will go up, everyone straight in.” 6 So Joshua son of Nun called the priests and said to them, “Take up the ark of the covenant of the LORD and have seven priests carry trumpets in front of it.” 7 And he ordered the army, “Advance! March around the city, with an armed guard going ahead of the ark of the LORD.” 8 When Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests carrying the seven trumpets before the LORD went forward, blowing their trumpets, and the ark of the LORD’s covenant followed them. 9 The armed guard marched ahead of the priests who blew the trumpets, and the rear guard followed the ark. All this time the trumpets were sounding. 10 But Joshua had commanded the army, “Do not give a war cry, do not raise your voices, do not say a word until the day I tell you to shout. Then shout!” 11 So he had the ark of the LORD carried around the city, circling it once. Then the army returned to camp and spent the night there. 12 Joshua got up early the next morning and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. 13 The seven priests carrying the seven trumpets went forward, marching before the ark of the LORD and blowing the trumpets. The armed men went ahead of them and the rear guard followed the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets kept sounding. 14 So on the second day they marched around the city once and returned to the camp. They did this for six days. 15 On the seventh day, they got up at daybreak and marched around the city seven times in the same manner, except that on that day they circled the city seven times. 16 The seventh time around, when the priests sounded the trumpet blast, Joshua commanded the army, “Shout! For the LORD has given you the city! 17 The city and all that is in it are to be devoted to the LORD. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall be spared, because she hid the spies we sent. 18 But keep away from the devoted things, so that you will not bring about your own destruction by taking any of them. Otherwise you will make the camp of Israel liable to destruction and bring trouble on it. 19 All the silver and gold and the articles of bronze and iron are sacred to the LORD and must go into his treasury.” 20 When the trumpets sounded, the army shouted, and at the sound of the trumpet, when the men gave a loud shout, the wall collapsed; so everyone charged straight in, and they took the city.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Josh 3:17.** NIV: the priests “stopped in the middle of the Jordan and stood on dry ground.” LSB: they “stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan.” They did not hurry out. They held their place until the whole nation had crossed.
- **Josh 6:2.** NIV: “I have delivered Jericho into your hands.” LSB: “I have given Jericho into your hand.” The city is spoken of as already given, before a single march.
- **Josh 6:5, 20.** NIV: “the wall of the city will collapse” and “the wall collapsed.” LSB: “the wall of the city will fall down beneath itself” and “the wall fell down beneath itself.” The wall does not fall because Israel shoves it. It comes down under itself, at the Lord’s word.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Joshua guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-joshua/) shows the Jordan parting like the sea, and Jericho falling as Joshua obeys a plan that does not make human sense, because this is God’s battle. John Piper’s sermon [“Faith to Be Strong and Faith to Be Weak”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/faith-to-be-strong-and-faith-to-be-weak) at Desiring God reads Hebrews 11:30 and says God works miracles through faith, without promising that he will always spare his people from suffering.

**Reflection question:** The priests stepped into a flooded river because the Lord went first, and Israel marched around Jericho because he had already given them the city. As a man, husband, and father, where is God asking you to obey a word that looks foolish, and to wait for him to do what only he can do?
